patients.label: 75-year-old retired man with depression and bipolar disorder after a declared intentional quetiapine overdose with QT prolongation and cardiac arrest
attribution_limitations: The ingested amount is 28 g in the text (280 pills of 100 mg, repeated in the abstract, the Table 1 caption and the conclusion) but Table 3 prints 2800 mg for this case, one digit short of 28000 mg. This is treated as a one-character print artefact (ambiguity, not a source conflict): the 2800 mg side is review_only and the text dose stays included. The discussion figures "about 24.5 g/28 g" absorbed and a dosage of "about 24 g" are author estimates of the absorbed amount, not the ingested amount, and are not reconciled. The Table 1 caption calls the ingestion "assumed".

Table 3 gives hour-labelled findings for this case after the overdose (loss of consciousness at 3 h, comatose at 5h, QT prolongation, chest pain and cardiac arrest at 9 h, QT prolongation at 24 h, normal conditions at 48 h). The text places the chest pain and cardiac arrest in the emergency room on arrival by ambulance, dates the first serum sample to about 4 h after intoxication, and says the QT-interval normalized after resuscitation maneuvers, whereas Table 3 still lists QT prolongation at 24 h. The source does not identify the table findings with the text events and gives no time for the normalization, so both are kept as separate items, the 24 h QT prolongation is not read as contradicting the normalization, and no order is asserted between the two chains other than both following the overdose.

The first serum sample is dated by the patient declaration to about 4 h after intoxication, whereas Table 1 times are relative to admission. No absolute offset from ingestion is derived for the Table 1 values.

The abstract refers to analysis from admission to discharge, but no discharge date, disposition or hospital length of stay is stated; Table 1 ends at 72 h after admission. No discharge outcome is recorded.

The increase in serum concentration between 36 and 48 h is attributed to hepatic redistribution only as a probable cause, and the possibility of nonlinear kinetics is discussed from other authors; no cause is asserted for this patient.
